Most translations switch to 'betray' when Judas is the subject, which is a fair description of the act but hides the chain of handings-over that runs through the narrative. Greek had a separate word for 'betray'."},{"verse":5,"phrase":"sanctuary","lemma":"ναός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temple","note":"Greek has two words that are usually both translated 'temple': one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one, for the sanctuary building itself. Most translations do not distinguish them. How Judas could throw coins into a building only priests entered is unclear; Matthew may be using the word loosely or echoing Zechariah 11:13, where the silver is thrown into the house of the Lord."},{"verse":9,"phrase":"Jeremiah the prophet","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"The words quoted are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, not to any passage in Jeremiah. The usual explanation is that Matthew combines Zechariah with Jeremiah's passages about a potter, innocent blood and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32) and names the better-known prophet. The question remains debated."},{"verse":11,"phrase":"You say so","lemma":"λέγω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"","note":"Literally 'You are saying it.' The reply neither denies the title nor plainly claims it. It can be heard as a guarded yes ('it is as you say') or as putting the words back on Pilate ('that is your way of putting it'). Most interpreters take it as a qualified affirmation; the translation leaves it as open as the Greek."},{"verse":16,"phrase":"Jesus Barabbas","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"Barabbas","note":"Most manuscripts read simply 'Barabbas' here and in verse 17. The Greek edition translated here prints 'Jesus Barabbas' in both places, a reading found in a small number of witnesses and known to Origen in the third century. Many scholars think copyists dropped the name 'Jesus' out of reverence, but the matter is not settled, and some editions mark the name as doubtful."},{"verse":17,"phrase":"Messiah","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"Christ","note":"Pilate is referring to a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not to a surname. 'Messiah' lets a modern reader hear that. This translation keeps 'Christ' where the word works as part of Jesus's name, and several modern translations make the same distinction."},{"verse":25,"phrase":"His blood be on us and on our children!","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"The wording is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16). Many interpreters think Matthew has in view the generation that lived to see Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70. The verse was later used to blame Jews of every age for the death of Jesus, a use that goes well beyond what the narrative says."},{"verse":38,"phrase":"bandits","lemma":"λῃστής","kind":"departure","traditional":"thieves / robbers","note":"The word means someone who takes by violence, a brigand or bandit; Greek had a different word for a sneak thief. Josephus often uses it for armed rebels, and because crucifixion was a Roman penalty for sedition, some scholars think these men were insurrectionists. That is possible but not certain. Some modern translations also have 'bandits' or 'rebels'."},{"verse":45,"phrase":"the sixth hour","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated 'land' can also mean 'earth'; most translations take it to mean the region."},{"verse":46,"phrase":"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"This is the opening line of Psalm 22, given first in Semitic words and then in Greek. The psalm is echoed several times in this chapter: the dividing of clothes by lot (v. 35), the shaking of heads (v. 39) and the taunt 'He trusts in God; let God rescue him' (v. 43). The bystanders' confusion with Elijah turns on the sound of 'Eli'."},{"verse":52,"phrase":"holy ones","lemma":"ἅγιος","kind":"departure","traditional":"saints","note":"'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means those set apart for God, and here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'holy people'."},{"verse":54,"phrase":"God’s Son","lemma":"υἱός","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"the Son of God","note":"The Greek has no article and could be translated 'a son of a god', which is what a Roman soldier might naturally have meant. Greek does not need the article here to carry the definite sense, and Matthew uses the same article-less phrase in the taunt of verse 43, which the soldiers' words answer. Most translations have 'the Son of God'; 'God's Son' keeps the echo and something of the openness."},{"verse":62,"phrase":"the Preparation","lemma":"παρασκευή","kind":"background","traditional":"","note":"'Preparation' was the ordinary Jewish name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. Matthew's roundabout phrase therefore means the Sabbath itself. Why he avoids naming it is uncertain."},{"verse":65,"phrase":"You have a guard","lemma":"ἔχω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"","note":"The Greek verb form can be a statement ('You have a guard') or a command ('Take a guard'). As a statement it may mean that Pilate is granting them soldiers, or that he is telling them to use their own temple police. The Latin loanword used for 'guard' and the soldiers' answerability to the governor in 28:14 suggest Roman troops, but the point is disputed."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"παραδίδωμι","rendering":"hand over","verse":2,"reason":"Translations alternate between 'betray', 'hand over' and 'deliver up' for the same verb across the passion narratives and Paul, hiding a deliberate verbal thread."},{"lemma":"ναός","rendering":"sanctuary","verse":5,"reason":"It needs a consistent distinction from ἱερόν (the whole temple complex) across the Gospels, Paul's 'temple of God' language and Revelation."},{"lemma":"λῃστής","rendering":"bandit","verse":38,"reason":"It is rendered variously as thief, robber, bandit or rebel across the Gospels (including 'den of robbers' and Barabbas in John), and the choice affects how readers understand those crucified with Jesus."},{"lemma":"ἐγείρω","rendering":"raise / be raised","verse":52,"reason":"Whether the passive is rendered 'was raised' or 'rose' recurs in every resurrection passage and should be decided once."},{"lemma":"διακονέω","rendering":"serve","verse":55,"reason":"It is rendered variously as 'minister to', 'serve', 'provide for' and 'wait on' across the New Testament, and the choice shapes how readers see the women's role and later church offices."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people reached a decision against Jesus, to put him to death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Judas, who had handed him over, seeing that Jesus had been condemned, was seized with remorse and returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Throwing the silver coins into the sanctuary, he withdrew, and he went away and hanged himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests took the silver coins and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not lawful to put them into the temple treasury, since they are the price of blood.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, having reached a decision, they used them to buy the Potter’s Field as a burial place for foreigners.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And they took the thirty silver coins, the price of the one who was priced, whom some of the sons of Israel had priced,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say so.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And while he was being accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pilate said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you not hear how many things they are testifying against you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now at the festival the governor was accustomed to release one prisoner to the crowd, whichever one they wanted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Jesus Barabbas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whom do you want me to release to you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called the Messiah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he knew that it was out of envy that they had handed him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much today in a dream because of him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The governor asked them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Barabbas.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called the Messiah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let him be crucified!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why, what evil has he done?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they shouted all the more,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let him be crucified!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, and that instead a riot was starting, he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am innocent of this man’s blood. See to it yourselves.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the people answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “His blood be on us and on our children!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he released Barabbas to them; and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole cohort around him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak on him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after twisting together a crown of thorns they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Hail, king of the Jews!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they spat on him, took the reed, and kept striking him on the head.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; they pressed him into service to carry his cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; but when he had tasted it, he refused to drink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by casting lots,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they sat down and kept watch over him there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Above his head they put the charge against him in writing: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then two bandits were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those passing by hurled abuse at him, shaking their heads

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are God’s Son, come down from the cross!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the chief priests also, along with the scribes and elders, mocked him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. He is the king of Israel! Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He trusts in God; let God rescue him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am God’s Son.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the bandits who were crucified with him also taunted him in the same way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of those standing there, when they heard it, said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is calling Elijah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once one of them ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the rest said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, the curtain of the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom, the earth shook, the rocks were split,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the holy ones who had fallen asleep were raised,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were terrified and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Truly this man was God’s Son!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many women were there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who had himself also become a disciple of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, that is, the day after the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will be raised.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So give orders for the tomb to be made secure until the third day; otherwise his disciples may come and steal him and tell the people, ‘He has been raised from the dead,’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you know how.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they went and made the tomb secure with the guard, after sealing the stone.

notes.note: The Greek verb means to hand over or deliver up. It is the same word used when the priests hand Jesus to Pilate (v. 2) and when Pilate hands him over to be crucified (v. 26). Most translations switch to 'betray' when Judas is the subject, which is a fair description of the act but hides the chain of handings-over that runs through the narrative. Greek had a separate word for 'betray'.

Greek has two words that are usually both translated 'temple': one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one, for the sanctuary building itself. Most translations do not distinguish them. How Judas could throw coins into a building only priests entered is unclear; Matthew may be using the word loosely or echoing Zechariah 11:13, where the silver is thrown into the house of the Lord.

The words quoted are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, not to any passage in Jeremiah. The usual explanation is that Matthew combines Zechariah with Jeremiah's passages about a potter, innocent blood and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32) and names the better-known prophet. The question remains debated.

Literally 'You are saying it.' The reply neither denies the title nor plainly claims it. It can be heard as a guarded yes ('it is as you say') or as putting the words back on Pilate ('that is your way of putting it'). Most interpreters take it as a qualified affirmation; the translation leaves it as open as the Greek.

Most manuscripts read simply 'Barabbas' here and in verse 17. The Greek edition translated here prints 'Jesus Barabbas' in both places, a reading found in a small number of witnesses and known to Origen in the third century. Many scholars think copyists dropped the name 'Jesus' out of reverence, but the matter is not settled, and some editions mark the name as doubtful.

Pilate is referring to a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not to a surname. 'Messiah' lets a modern reader hear that. This translation keeps 'Christ' where the word works as part of Jesus's name, and several modern translations make the same distinction.

notes.phrase: His blood be on us and on our children!
notes.note: The wording is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16). Many interpreters think Matthew has in view the generation that lived to see Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70. The verse was later used to blame Jews of every age for the death of Jesus, a use that goes well beyond what the narrative says.

The word means someone who takes by violence, a brigand or bandit; Greek had a different word for a sneak thief. Josephus often uses it for armed rebels, and because crucifixion was a Roman penalty for sedition, some scholars think these men were insurrectionists. That is possible but not certain. Some modern translations also have 'bandits' or 'rebels'.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated 'land' can also mean 'earth'; most translations take it to mean the region.

notes.phrase: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
notes.note: This is the opening line of Psalm 22, given first in Semitic words and then in Greek. The psalm is echoed several times in this chapter: the dividing of clothes by lot (v. 35), the shaking of heads (v. 39) and the taunt 'He trusts in God; let God rescue him' (v. 43). The bystanders' confusion with Elijah turns on the sound of 'Eli'.

'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means those set apart for God, and here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'holy people'.

The Greek has no article and could be translated 'a son of a god', which is what a Roman soldier might naturally have meant. Greek does not need the article here to carry the definite sense, and Matthew uses the same article-less phrase in the taunt of verse 43, which the soldiers' words answer. Most translations have 'the Son of God'; 'God's Son' keeps the echo and something of the openness.
'Preparation' was the ordinary Jewish name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. Matthew's roundabout phrase therefore means the Sabbath itself. Why he avoids naming it is uncertain.

The Greek verb form can be a statement ('You have a guard') or a command ('Take a guard'). As a statement it may mean that Pilate is granting them soldiers, or that he is telling them to use their own temple police. The Latin loanword used for 'guard' and the soldiers' answerability to the governor in 28:14 suggest Roman troops, but the point is disputed.

candidates.reason: Translations alternate between 'betray', 'hand over' and 'deliver up' for the same verb across the passion narratives and Paul, hiding a deliberate verbal thread.
It needs a consistent distinction from ἱερόν (the whole temple complex) across the Gospels, Paul's 'temple of God' language and Revelation.

It is rendered variously as thief, robber, bandit or rebel across the Gospels (including 'den of robbers' and Barabbas in John), and the choice affects how readers understand those crucified with Jesus.
Whether the passive is rendered 'was raised' or 'rose' recurs in every resurrection passage and should be decided once.
It is rendered variously as 'minister to', 'serve', 'provide for' and 'wait on' across the New Testament, and the choice shapes how readers see the women's role and later church offices.
